title: CR-18 / Module 2 / N2d — External Network Enumeration
description: Route into a client's public /28 assessment range from an external vantage point, fingerprint every exposed edge service with ICMP filtered, and correlate certificate metadata across a web gateway, mail server, and VPN endpoint to uncover a hostname the client never intended to disclose. Concludes with a short knowledge-check assessment.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with TCP/IP networking (routing, ports, common services)
No prior nmap, openssl, ffuf, or ike-scan experience required — covered in the background level
outcomes: Determine network routing/gateway paths to an external assessment range
Perform host and service discovery when ICMP-based discovery is filtered
Enumerate TLS certificates for disclosed hostnames beyond the Common Name (Subject Alternative Names)
Fuzz virtual hosts across HTTP/HTTPS services to uncover hidden site configurations
Fingerprint VPN/IKE services and correlate findings across multiple external hosts

levels.title: Introduction level
levels.content:
Welcome to the External Network Reconnaissance & Enumeration lab.

Cadmus Corp has commissioned an external perimeter assessment. All you've been given is a single fact: their public assessment range is `203.0.113.0/28`. No host list, no service map — you're working purely from the outside in, exactly as an attacker would.

From your assessment workstation you'll work out how traffic actually reaches that range, sweep it for live hosts (a sweep will not show you all of them), and fingerprint every edge service you find. At least one system on this perimeter answers nothing your default probes send, and it is not the least interesting box in the range. Certificates in particular tend to say more than their owners intend — a Common Name is rarely the whole story. Somewhere in this range, a TLS certificate discloses a hostname that was never meant to be public.

You have **30 minutes** for the scanning exercise. A short background level right after you get access covers every tool you'll need if you haven't used them before. A 10-minute knowledge-check follows once you're done — by then you'll already have everything you need to answer it from your own scan output.

levels.title: Background — external scanning tools
levels.content:
No target list is provided for this exercise beyond the assessment range itself. Everything below is tool syntax you may need; working out which applies where — and noticing when a tool's default behaviour is quietly failing you — is the exercise.

## Routing

    ip route get <target_ip>          # shows exactly which gateway your traffic uses to reach a target

## nmap

    sudo nmap -sn <range>              # host discovery — ICMP echo plus TCP probes to 443 and 80
    nmap -Pn -p <ports> <target_ip>    # scan WITHOUT host discovery — use this if a target or range that
                                        # should be live shows nothing with -sn
    sudo nmap -Pn -sS -p- <target_ip>  # full TCP port range (all 65535) — the default top-1000 scan can
                                        # miss services running on unusual high ports
    sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC <target_ip>  # version detection + default scripts on whatever ports you specify
    sudo nmap -Pn -sU -p <ports> <target_ip>   # UDP scan — always narrow the port range first, it's slow
    nmap -Pn -p <port> --script ssl-cert <target_ip>     # dump a TLS certificate's fields, including SANs
    nmap -Pn -p 25 --script smtp-commands <target_ip>    # enumerate SMTP capabilities and the server banner

## openssl — inspecting TLS certificates directly

    openssl s_client -connect <target_ip>:<port> -servername <hostname> </dev/null 2>/dev/null | \
        openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName

The `-subject` line shows the certificate's Common Name (CN). The `-ext subjectAltName` line shows every OTHER hostname the certificate is valid for — a certificate frequently discloses more names than the one you connected with.

## ffuf — virtual host fuzzing

    ffuf -w <wordlist> -u http://<target_ip>/ -H "Host: FUZZ.<domain>" -k -ac

If a web server hosts multiple sites behind one IP, distinguishable only by the `Host:` header, a wordlist fuzzed against that header can surface virtual hosts a normal browse-through would never reveal. Run it against every HTTP/HTTPS port you find, not just port 80.

## ike-scan — fingerprinting VPN/IKE services

    sudo ike-scan --ikev2 <target_ip>

If UDP/500 is open and nmap identifies it as `isakmp`, this confirms the IKE version in use and is usually the fastest way to get a clean answer, faster than parsing nmap's own guesses.

levels.title: Map the Perimeter
levels.content:
All you have is the range: `203.0.113.0/28`. Everything else is yours to find.

Your objectives for this level:

* Work out which gateway your traffic actually uses to reach that range.
* Sweep the range for live hosts.

*Note: a default sweep tells you which hosts answered, not which hosts exist. Check the count against the size of the range and confirm the gaps before you decide your list is complete.*

* Once you have live hosts, scan each one thoroughly — not just the handful of ports a default scan checks. Services sometimes sit on ports nobody expects to look at.
* One of the hosts you find runs a VPN service. Fingerprint it, then inspect whatever TLS certificate it presents. Certificates often disclose more hostnames than the one you connected with.

Submit the **alternate hostname disclosed in that VPN host's TLS certificate** as your answer for this stage.

*Note: the knowledge-check after this level draws on findings from every host you scan, not just the VPN endpoint — cover the whole range, not just enough to find the flag.*
levels.solution:
* Check your route — `ip route get 203.0.113.5` → traffic goes via gateway 198.51.100.1.
* Sweep the range — `sudo nmap -sn 203.0.113.0/28` → finds the gateway, the web gateway and the VPN endpoint, but not the mail server, which permits only its own service ports and drops everything else.
* Re-scan without relying on host discovery — `nmap -Pn -p 80,443,25,587 <candidate_ip>` across the range → the mail server answers on its own ports once `-Pn` stops it being skipped.
* Scan each live host for service details: `sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC <ip>`. One host (203.0.113.13) shows TCP/443; adding a UDP scan (`sudo nmap -Pn -sU -p 500,4500 203.0.113.13`) reveals UDP/500 and UDP/4500 — a VPN gateway.
* Inspect its HTTPS certificate for disclosed names:
```
openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.13:443 -servername vpn.cadmus-corp.lab </dev/null 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName
```
The CN is `vpn.cadmus-corp.lab`; the SAN list additionally discloses `remote.cadmus-corp.lab`.

**Answer: remote.cadmus-corp.lab**

hints.title: Trust Nothing That Comes Back Empty
hints.content: Compare the number of hosts your sweep found against the size of the range. If the count is short, the gap is a host that is not answering the probes discovery relies on. `-Pn` skips discovery entirely and scans an address regardless of whether it replied.

hints.title: Scan Past the Defaults
hints.content:
A default nmap scan only checks the top 1000 ports. If a host's most interesting service sits above that, you'll never see it without explicitly scanning the full range.

Useful flags: `-Pn` (skip host discovery), `-p-` (all 65535 ports).

hints.title: Certificates Say More Than You Asked
hints.content:
A TLS certificate's Common Name is only ever one name among possibly several. Look at the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field on any certificate you find — especially on services that feel administrative or remote-access-related.

Useful tool: `openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName`, or nmap's `ssl-cert` script.

hints.title: Full Sequence for the VPN Host
hints.content:
```
sudo nmap -Pn -sU -p 500,4500 <target_ip>
sudo ike-scan --ikev2 <target_ip>
openssl s_client -connect <target_ip>:443 -servername vpn.cadmus-corp.lab </dev/null 2>/dev/null | \
    openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName
```
The SAN field carries the answer.

levels.title: Knowledge Check

questions.text: What gateway does your traffic use to reach 203.0.113.0/28?
Excluding the gateway, how many hosts did you find in 203.0.113.0/28 once you scanned past filtered discovery?
Which nmap option lets you scan a target without relying on host discovery?
What web-server software is exposed on 203.0.113.5's web ports?
What Common Name (CN) is present in the TLS certificate served on 203.0.113.5:443?
Beyond 80 and 443, 203.0.113.5 serves one further TLS port. What alternate management hostname does the certificate on that port disclose in its SAN field?
Which TCP port on 203.0.113.9 is used for SMTP Submission?
What hostname does 203.0.113.9 identify itself as during SMTP enumeration?
Which version of IKE does 203.0.113.13 present on UDP/500?
Which service does nmap identify on 203.0.113.13's UDP/500?

levels.instructions: Answer using what you already found while scanning in the previous level — no new scanning is required. Ten questions cover findings from across every host you enumerated, not just the VPN endpoint. Hosts are referenced by IP, the same way you found them. You have 10 minutes.

levels.title: Lab Completed
levels.content: You've completed the External Network Reconnaissance & Enumeration lab. Starting from a single /28 range and nothing else, you worked out your own routing path, adapted when host discovery was filtered, scanned past the defaults to find services on unusual ports, and correlated certificate metadata across three hosts to surface a hostname the client never intended to expose. This is exactly how a real external assessment starts — not with a target list, but with a range and the discipline to check everything twice. Head back to the LMS to continue the course.
